chapter_metadata.title: Bronchoscopic Management of Persistent Air Leaks
chapter_metadata.reference: Principles and Practice of Interventional Pulmonology, 2025

definitions.definition: Air leak persisting >5 days due to bronchopleural or alveolar‑pleural fistula.
Communication between bronchial tree and pleural space; may be central or peripheral.
Communication between alveoli and pleural space.
Ventilation between segments/lobes via collateral channels that can mask leak localization.

technology_and_technique.summary: Deep sedation or general anesthesia preferred. Use large endotracheal tube (≥8.0 mm), laryngeal mask, or rigid bronchoscope; closed‑circuit ventilation helps quantify air leak.
Sequential balloon occlusion from lobe to segments to subsegments; wait several cycles; balloon ≥1 min to confirm air leak decrease and reincrease on deflation. CV can blunt effect.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Sequential balloon occlusion
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Localize lobe/segments feeding PAL to minimize number of occluded subsegments.
steps: Occlude main lobe entrance; observe pleural drainage device for air leak reduction.
If no change, test other ipsilateral lobes; if reduction, proceed segmentally within involved lobe.
Hold occlusion ≥60 seconds; verify reincrease after deflation.
Aim to block the least number of segments that abolish the leak.
diagnostic_approaches.notes: Perform inspection bronchoscopy first; obtain wash; document visible fistulas if present.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Reverse‑flow oxygen insufflation
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Detect occult contributors when airflow ceases under anesthesia.
steps: Attach low‑flow O2 to bronchoscope suction port.
Deliver brief insufflation bursts (press suction valve) to increase flow in selected airway.
A rise suggests contribution to PAL.
diagnostic_approaches.notes: Useful when supine position/general anesthesia reduce spontaneous airflow.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Methylene blue tracing
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Track communication between bronchial segments and pleural space.
variants: Instill via chest drain and observe appearance in bronchial tree.
Instill endobronchially and observe dye at chest tube.

clinical_procedures.name: Endobronchial one‑way valve placement (EBV/SVS)
devices: Spiration Valve System (Olympus; FDA‑authorized for PAL)
steps: Size airway using deployment system; choose valve size.
Place valve(s) to occlude all contributing segments.
Confirm air leak reduction at chest drainage device; adjust as needed.

clinical_procedures.name: Watanabe spigot (EWS) bronchial occlusion
indications: Peripheral BPF/PAL in small to moderate bronchi
steps: Select spigot size; advance to target segment.
Wedge and seat securely; reassess air leak.
Combine with chemical pleurodesis when appropriate.

clinical_procedures.name: Tissue adhesives/sealants
indications: Selected peripheral fistulas where devices unsuitable
notes: Form clot/plug; fibrin glue degrades in ~14 days
clinical_procedures.evidence: Case series/reports; high success in smaller fistulas

recommendations: Initial therapy: chest tube drainage; most PALs resolve within 14 days.
Primary spontaneous: ~75% resolve within 7 days and 100% by 15 days; Secondary spontaneous: 61% at 7 days, 79% at 14 days.
Consider thoracic suction; larger‑bore drains (20–32 Fr) for ongoing PAL.
Consider pleurodesis (talc or autologous blood patch) via chest tube for nonsurgical candidates.
Outpatient Heimlich valve may be used with close follow‑up.
Surgical evaluation recommended (VATS preferred when feasible); bullectomy/pleurodesis reduce recurrence.
Localize with balloon occlusion before definitive bronchoscopic therapy.
Use general anesthesia and closed‑circuit ventilation when deploying valves.

mitigation: Careful sizing; surveillance bronchoscopy if indicated

Aim to occlude the fewest segments

Reassess leak and lung expansion; plan removal if healed

summary: Begin with drainage optimization and pleurodesis options; obtain surgical consult.
If surgery not feasible, localize PAL bronchoscopically and occlude the minimal necessary segments.
Select device/adhesive based on anatomy and risk; reassess for healing and remove devices when feasible.

points: PALs are challenging; most resolve with drainage within 1–2 weeks, but a subset needs advanced therapy.
Sequential balloon occlusion with adjunct maneuvers enables targeted bronchoscopic closure with valves, spigots, stents, or adhesives.
Collateral ventilation and anesthesia effects complicate localization; structured workflows improve success.
